author: Carlos Martinez
title: Iowa Speedway iRacing Guide: Setup, Line, and Wet Weather
description: Master Iowa's tight oval with detailed brake zones, throttle application, and setup adjustments for the MOZA R9. Learn the racing line and fuel strategy.

sections.p: Iowa Speedway is one of iRacing's most punishing ovals—a short, flat, high-banked D-shaped track where precision matters more than raw speed. I've spent dozens of hours there with my MOZA R9 setup, and every lap teaches me something about brake modulation and throttle discipline. The banking is deceptive; it looks forgiving until you overdrive the entry and scrub speed into the wall. This guide walks you through the racing line, setup adjustments, and the fuel management strategy that keeps you out of the pits.

Iowa's 7/8-mile layout and steep ~14° banking make it feel faster than it is, but the real challenge is consistency. The racing line is tight, the corner radii are sharp, and traffic is constant. Get the fundamentals right first—line, braking points, throttle application—before chasing lap time.

sections.h2: The Racing Line and Brake Points

sections.p: Iowa has two corners, and they define everything you do here. Turn 1 is a long, sweeping right-hander; Turn 2 is a shorter left. The banking helps you carry speed, but only if you're smooth and patient.

I brake around marker 4 on the backmarker (the painted line on the apron), which puts me roughly 400 feet before the corner. My initial brake pressure is high—around 85% on my MOZA CRP2 load cell—to scrub speed quickly. The key is to avoid trail-braking too deep; Iowa rewards a late, stabbed brake application rather than prolonged pressure into the turn. Once I've hit my target speed (usually ~155 mph in a Cup car), I release the brake cleanly and turn in.

The entry is wide. I start near the white line on the outside and immediately use the banking to hold the arc. Smooth steering input is critical; any jerky correction upsets the car and kills your exit speed. I aim to hit the bottom of the track around the apex—roughly the gray apron—and focus on a clean, rolling throttle application through the middle of the turn.

Throttle application at the exit is gradual. I start light (maybe 30% throttle) about halfway through the turn and build to full throttle by the time I'm 3/4 of the way through. The banking wants to push you up toward the wall, so I use that—I let the car roll higher as I add throttle. By the time I'm exiting, I'm near the wall at the top of the track, which is the correct line here. Full throttle down the front straightaway, holding the high line.

Turn 2 is shorter and tighter than Turn 1, which surprises drivers used to superspeedway racing. I brake around marker 1 on the backmarker, roughly 350 feet before the corner. Brake pressure is similar to Turn 1—a stabbed application to ~80% rather than trail-braking. I want to be off the brakes and turning by the time I reach the 30-yard line (the next marker).

The racing line is tighter here. I enter wider than I do in Turn 1, but I'm aiming for a more aggressive apex near the inside. Turn in early, use the banking to hold the arc, and focus on throttle application through the middle. Exit is where you gain or lose time; a bad exit will kill your speed down the back straightaway.

Throttle application mirrors Turn 1—gradual, rolling, building to full by the time you're three-quarters through the turn. Exit high toward the wall and maintain full throttle down the back straightaway. The back straightaway is shorter than the front, so you'll be braking for Turn 1 again quickly. This is where traffic becomes critical; you need clean air to hit your braking point.

sections.tip: Iowa rewards a stabbed brake input over trail-braking. Practice hitting your braking zones with a quick, decisive pressure application—85% for Turn 1, 80% for Turn 2—rather than easing in over 200+ feet. You'll stop shorter and preserve momentum into the corner.

sections.h2: Setup Tuning for Your MOZA Rig

sections.p: My MOZA R9 direct drive wheelbase (~9 N·m peak torque) gives me enough force feedback to feel the banking and weight transfer. Iowa setup is about balance; you need enough front wing to slow down without overdoing it, and enough rear wing to maintain stability.

list: Front wing: Start at ~8-10° for Cup cars. Too much creates drag and kills your straightaway speed; too little and you'll understeer into the corners. I usually run ~9° and adjust based on traffic.
Rear wing: ~6-8° for oval racing. The banking helps; you don't need excessive downforce. I run ~6-7° and only increase if I'm pushing hard into the walls.
Gear ratio: Iowa is all about top speed on the straightaways. Run a gear ratio that maxes out around 180-185 mph on the front straightaway (you'll be fuel-limited before you run out of gear).
Brake bias: ~55-60% front bias. Iowa's straights are short, so you don't need extreme braking power. I run ~57% and adjust if I'm locking the fronts or pushing through the corners.
Fuel consumption: This is critical. A fuel stint at Iowa lasts ~45 laps. Plan your pit strategy accordingly; I usually stop every 40 laps to be safe.

sections.p: Iowa is a momentum track. Every ounce of speed you carry through the corners carries down the straightaway. I focus on smooth throttle application, especially off Turn 2. A herky-jerky throttle input upsets the car and kills your drive off the corner.

Full throttle is your default state except during braking zones. Even during corner entry and middle, I'm looking to minimize lift-off. If I'm lifting in the middle of the turn, my brake point was too late or my entry speed was too high. Adjust brake markers or brake pressure, not your throttle application mid-corner.

Fuel consumption at Iowa is roughly ~0.8-0.9 gallons per lap in a Cup car. A standard fuel tank holds ~18 gallons, which gives you ~18-22 laps of fuel. In practice, I run stints of ~40-45 laps by pitting every 2 hours (calendar time), which accounts for cautions and traffic.

Plan your first stop around lap 40 if you're running a full fuel load. If you're practicing or qualifying, you might run 20-25 laps before needing to pit. In a race, cautions will extend your fuel stints; always save 2-3 laps of fuel as a buffer for the final laps.

sections.tip: Use the MoTeC telemetry export to calculate your exact fuel burn per lap. Iowa fuel consumption varies by setup (lower wing = lower fuel burn), so dial it in during practice. A quick stint of 20 laps at race pace will give you a precise number to use for race planning.

sections.p: Rain at Iowa changes everything. The banking becomes dangerous; a lot of drivers lift off and lose the car. Your approach shifts from speed to stability.

list: Brake earlier and softer in rain. Iowa's wet braking zones need ~100 feet more space than dry. Hit Turn 1 around marker 5 (instead of marker 4) and ease your brake pressure to ~70% to avoid locking.

Slow your throttle application on exit. The banking doesn't help you in the rain; it actually pushes you up the track faster than your tires can handle. Build throttle gradually and expect your car to climb the banking.
Run higher downforce in the wet. I add ~3-4° of wing on both ends to create grip. The reduced drag cost is worth the additional stability.
Avoid the apron. In the dry, the apron is the shortest line. In the wet, it's slicker and more treacherous. Stay on the main racing surface.

sections.p: Iowa is a short track with high field density. You'll spend a lot of time in traffic, and patience is your friend. Don't overdrive to pass on the first opportunity; wait for a clean zone with good spacing. A bad pass often leads to a spin or damaged aero, costing you 5-10 seconds.

When being passed, don't defend aggressively in the corners. Iowa's walls punish mistakes. Hang onto your line, let the passer make their move, and refocus on your own lap. If they miss their pass and make contact, that's on them. Your job is consistency.

Start by finding your baseline lap time: load a fresh setup, run 15-20 laps, and note your average pace. Then focus on the fundamentals in this order: first, nail your braking points; second, smooth out your throttle application; third, adjust setup to match your driving style. Only after all three are dialed should you chase the absolute limit.

Iowa rewards patience and repetition. It's a track where a 0.05-second improvement usually comes from one perfect lap, not a sudden setup change. Practice the line, focus on smoothness, and trust the process.

faqs.q: What's the ideal brake pressure for Iowa?
faqs.a: Roughly 80-85% for both turns, applied as a quick stab rather than a prolonged trail-brake. Iowa's short corners don't reward extended braking; you want to scrub speed quickly and turn in cleanly. Use telemetry to dial in your exact brake pressure curve, and adjust based on tire wear and fuel load.

faqs.q: How much fuel do I need for a full race at Iowa?
faqs.a: A standard fuel tank (~18 gallons) gets you roughly 20-22 laps in a Cup car. Plan your first stop around lap 40 if you're running a full fuel load at the start. In a race with cautions, you'll need fewer stops. Always keep a 2-3 lap fuel buffer at the end in case of a late restart.

faqs.q: Should I trail-brake into Iowa's corners?
faqs.a: No. Iowa corners are too tight and too high-banked for aggressive trail-braking. Use a late, stabbed brake application to hit your target speed, then turn in cleanly. Trail-braking will only overdrive the corners and push you toward the wall. The banking doesn't forgive overdriving like a high-speed track does.

faqs.q: What setup changes help in the wet at Iowa?
faqs.a: Add 3-4 degrees of wing on both front and rear, soften your brake pressure to 65-70%, and brake 50-100 feet earlier than you do in the dry. The wet banking is dangerous; prioritize stability over speed. Also avoid the apron—it's much slicker than the main racing surface and offers no advantage in the rain.
